articles.title: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
articles.summary: Gavin Newsom called the remarks "deranged", but the White House said Trump was warning of the risk of a nuclear Iran.
articles.preview: Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego has sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly worded rebuttal from the White House. California Governor Gavin Newsom condemned the comment - made by Trump at a campaign rally in Nebraska - as "deranged and dangerous," while LA Mayor Karen Bass described them as threats and an attempt to "encourage attacks on American lives".
articles.body:
Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego has sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly worded rebuttal from the White House.

California Governor Gavin Newsom condemned the comment - made by Trump at a campaign rally in Nebraska - as "deranged and dangerous," while LA Mayor Karen Bass described them as threats and an attempt to "encourage attacks on American lives".

According to the White House, however, Trump was saying that American cities would have been threatened by Iran had he not launched a war there earlier this year.

Both LA and San Diego house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.

Trump, while speaking on Monday in Nebraska about the Iran conflict, said: "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego."

There were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made.

The morning after Trump's statement, Governor Newsom announced that the "dangerous - if not treasonous" statement had prompted him to direct California's State Threat Assessment Center to "monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the remarks as an invitation" to target California.

The agency is designed to detect and prevent security threats in the state.

San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote that the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his "reckless war talk".

Trump is yet to respond to the statements made by California's leaders.

In a post on X, White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung described the "media freakout" over Trump's comments as "not rooted in reality".

"He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung wrote. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money".

The president and other administration officials often claim that disrupting Iran's nuclear programme was essential for US national security, and that any issues that have stemmed from the conflict were necessary.

A separate X post, from the official White House rapid response account, described journalists from the Los Angeles Times reporting on the comments as "buffoons" and again pushed back on the characterisation of the comments by Newsom and others.

"He was saying the US is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon â which they would if they had the chance," the account added.

San Diego, located 17 miles (27km) from the border with Mexico, is the eighth largest city in the US and is home to Naval Base San Diego, the home port of the US Navy's Pacific Fleet, and Naval Amphibious Base Coronado - the main training centre Navy Seals on the West Coast.

It is also where Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton is located, a base which 70,000 service members and civilians work at.

Located approximately 120 miles (193 KM) north of San Diego, Los Angeles is the second most populous city in the US.

It is home to the space system command headquarters of the US Space Force, as well as the Los Angeles Air Force Base.

This not the first time the US president and California governor, who may run for president in 2028, have publicly clashed.

Last year Trump described him as incompetent, saying he had failed to adequately respond after some of the Los Angeles anti-immigration enforcement protests turned violent.

Newsom accused Trump of a "brazen abuse of power" after military personnel were deployed to secure federal buildings during those protests.

Earlier this year, Trump mocked Newsom's dyslexia, saying presidents should not have learning disabilities, which led to criticism from dyslexia charities.

articles.title: Ex-US spy who stashed gold bars in his home admits to $200m scam
articles.summary: David Rush, who also confessed to providing secrets to a foreign government, had revealed the existence of a "clandestine human source", prosecutors said.
articles.preview: A former CIA officer who was arrested after authorities found hundreds of gold bars stashed in his home has admitted to defrauding the US government in a sprawling $200m (£151m) scam involving fake contracts and real estate. David Rush, 49, is required to pay restitution to the government and forfeit luxury real estate, cars, watches and other assets tied to his crime as part of the plea deal. Rush also confessed to providing secrets to a foreign government, which could have caused "grave damage" to national security.
articles.body:
A former CIA officer who was arrested after authorities found hundreds of gold bars stashed in his home has admitted to defrauding the US government in a sprawling $200m (£151m) scam involving fake contracts and real estate.

David Rush, 49, is required to pay restitution to the government and forfeit luxury real estate, cars, watches and other assets tied to his crime as part of the plea deal.

Rush also confessed to providing secrets to a foreign government, which could have caused "grave damage" to national security.

"The defendant will plead guilty because the defendant is in fact guilty of the charged offense," prosecutors stated in a court filing outlining the plea deal.

The BBC has contacted Rush's lawyer, who declined to comment.

Rush was initially charged with theft of public funds, but has now pleaded guilty to wire fraud. At the time of his arrest, a raid on his home uncovered 298 gold bars that he had received for "work-related expenses".

Court filings around the deal bring new details to light, including that Rush revealed the existence and description of a "clandestine human source" to a foreign official.

"The disclosure of such information could endanger the safety and life of the human source and the US government officers working with the source and jeopardize the US government's ability to recruit human sources, who rely on the US government's assurances of absolute secrecy," prosecutors said in the filing.

In a news release, CIA Director John Ratcliffe said Rush "abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions".

FBI investigators said that between November 2025 to March 2026 Rush made repeated requests for "a significant quantity of foreign currency and tens of millions of dollars in gold bars for work-related expenses".

"Rush fabricated a highly classified program to justify the acquisition of luxury real estate in South Florida, which he then intended to resell for personal profit," the court filing laying out the deal states.

Rush "effectively acted as his own approving official, enabling him to expend substantial amounts of United States government money without meaningful scrutiny", according to the filing.

He then used "fraudulently obtained" public funds to acquire luxury real estate properties in southern Florida. According to the court filing, part of the scam included hiring an interior designer and purchasing $40,000 worth of kitchen appliances for one property.

The wire transfer charge was related to a $45m transfer that he initiated in January 2026. The plea deal also says that he provided top secret data to "a foreign government official who was not authorised to receive it and had no need to know it".

Along with the gold bars, Rush was also found with $2m in cash and 35 luxury watches.

Prosecutors said Rush was moving funds into commodities that could be easily traded, citing "strong evidence" he was trying to hide the money.

Under the deal, he is also required to turn in the watches and two BMW vehicles, along with the cash and nearly $39m that was seized from his bank account.

A federal judge will set his sentence at a later date, and a hearing has been scheduled for 28 January. The charge carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years, but prosecutors noted that the time can be added to under federal law.

In June, US Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick cited Rush's professional career in deciding he was a flight risk, and ordered him held in jail pending trial.

"He's in a different position than most people to flee and avoid detection by law enforcement," he said.

Court records do not go into detail about Rush's work for the CIA, and describe him as a former senior executive in a US government agency in Virginia who had top secret clearance and access to classified information.

US media have confirmed his former employment with the CIA. According to The Washington Post, external, he was senior executive in the agency's Directorate of Science and Technology, which develops high-tech spy tools.

He had also previously been accused of fraudulently taking military leave with pay after being honourably discharged from the US Navy, and for lying about his education and military service when applying for his job in 2009. Court records show Rush was accused of falsely telling employers he had been a navy pilot.

"These and other representations concerning Rush's military and academic accomplishments were false," the plea deal filing states.

It is unclear how he was able to lie on his application form, and according to The Washington Post, several CIA officials have been placed on leave as they investigate why he was able to pass a background check.

The government had argued previously that large sums of the funds are still unaccounted for, a claim which his lawyer has denied.

articles.title: Un’intera regione sprofondata nella guerra
articles.summary: Tre anni dopo l’attacco di Hamas contro Israele, il Medio Oriente è segnato da conflitti, fratture e tragedie, dalla Striscia di Gaza allo Yemen
articles.preview: Come le scosse di assestamento di un terremoto, che possono arrivare anche molto tempo dopo il sisma iniziale, il 7 ottobre 2023 continua a scuotere il Medio Oriente. A tre anni di distanza da quel giorno fatidico, il paesaggio regionale è segnato dalle guerre, dalle fratture e dai conflitti senza soluzione: da Rafah, nella Striscia di Gaza, a Hormuz, nel golfo Persico; da Naqura, nel sud del Libano, a Mocha, in Yemen. Tutto questo, evidentemente, non è cominciato il 7 ottobre.
articles.body:
Come le scosse di assestamento di un terremoto, che possono arrivare anche molto tempo dopo il sisma iniziale, il 7 ottobre 2023 continua a scuotere il Medio Oriente. A tre anni di distanza da quel giorno fatidico, il paesaggio regionale è segnato dalle guerre, dalle fratture e dai conflitti senza soluzione: da Rafah, nella Striscia di Gaza, a Hormuz, nel golfo Persico; da Naqura, nel sud del Libano, a Mocha, in Yemen.

Tutto questo, evidentemente, non è cominciato il 7 ottobre. La dinamica si era già messa in moto da tempo e ognuno dei conflitti citati ha vissuto numerosi episodi molto prima del 2023. Tuttavia, l’attacco di Hamas contro le comunità del sud di Israele – con il suo carattere inedito, la sua portata, il gran numero di vittime civili, la cattura di numerosi ostaggi e lefalle nella sicurezza dello stato ebraico – è stato un punto di rottura in questa regione martoriata.

Fin dai primi giorni è apparso chiaro che Israele avrebbe risposto subito al più grave attacco terroristico dalla sua nascita. Sapevamo che questa risposta sarebbe stata sproporzionata, perché questa è la dottrina dell’esercito israeliano. Presto abbiamo scoperto anche che sarebbe stata impietosa, sull’onda della sete di vendetta e dell’idea che a Gaza non ci fossero “innocenti”.

Ma a pagarne il prezzo non sono stati solo gli abitanti della Striscia. Anche il Libano è stato trascinato nella guerra quando Hezbollah, movimento armato sciita e filoisraeliano, ha voluto manifestare la propria solidarietà ad Hamas. Nel 2024, e poi di nuovo quest’anno, il Libano si è ritrovato sotto le bombe israeliane, mentre gli abitanti del nord di Israele hanno dovuto affrontare i razzi di Hezbollah. Oggi il Libano è in un’impasse, incapace di disarmare Hezbollah e alle prese con un’occupazione prolungata del sud del paese da parte delle forze israeliane. Una tragedia, per uno stato ormai esangue.

La vera svolta, però, è arrivata con la guerra scatenata da Israele e dagli Stati Uniti contro l’Iran, con una violenza mai vista in passato. Prima c’è stata la cosiddetta guerra dei dodici giorni, nel 2025. Poi, con bombardamenti ancora più massicci, è arrivata l’offensiva dello scorso febbraio, che ha decapitato il regime iraniano, uccidendo la guida suprema Ali Khamenei.

Da allora Donald Trump, con la sua incompetenza, si è impantanato sempre di più in una guerra da cui non riesce a uscire e che ha intaccato la credibilità della potenza statunitense nella regione.

Una soluzione a breve termine per questi conflitti non esiste. Al contrario, la guerra si sta allargando allo Yemen, con il coinvolgimento dell’Arabia Saudita che difende le sue esportazioni petrolifere. Nel frattempo la violenza dei coloni in Cisgiordania continua a crescere, il calvario di Gaza prosegue e un’intera regione vive il terzo anno di tempesta.

L’unico elemento che potrebbe fermare questa spirale infernale è l’esito delle elezioni israeliane, previste fra tre settimane. Ma davvero gli elettori dello stato ebraico decideranno di punire il primo ministro Benjamin Netanyahu per la sua responsabilità in queste tragedie? O si affideranno ancora una volta a lui (ciecamente, verrebbe da dire)?

Gli oppositori di Netanyahu non sono certo moderati sulla questione palestinese, ma resta il fatto che una sua eventuale uscita di scena, insieme alla sua coalizione di estrema destra, cambierebbe le carte in tavola, permettendo, forse, di voltare finalmente la pagina tragica aperta il 7 ottobre 2023.

(Traduzione di Andrea Sparacino)

Internazionale pubblica ogni settimana una pagina di lettere. Ci piacerebbe sapere cosa pensi di questo articolo. Scrivici a: posta@internazionale.it

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis attack Aden airport; Saudi forces down missile near Riyadh
articles.summary: Yemeni government says one of the missiles hit Aden airport's runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land.
articles.preview: Yemeni government says one of the missiles hit Aden airport’s runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land. Two Houthi missiles target Yemen’s Aden International Airport Yemen’s internationally recognised government has accused the Houthis of firing ballistic missiles and drones at the main international airport under its control, as Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted another missile north of its capital, Riyadh.
articles.body:
Yemeni government says one of the missiles hit Aden airport’s runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land.

Two Houthi missiles target Yemen’s Aden International Airport

Yemen’s internationally recognised government has accused the Houthis of firing ballistic missiles and drones at the main international airport under its control, as Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted another missile north of its capital, Riyadh.

In a statement on Wednesday, the Ministry of Transport said the Houthis targeted the runway and passenger terminal at the airport with at least two ballistic missiles and several drones.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

- list 1 of 3Yemen forces claim key gains near Bab al-Mandeb: What’s the latest?

- list 2 of 3Yemen’s government is on the attack against the Houthis. What has changed?

- list 3 of 3Yemeni forces launch offensive to retake Houthi-held al-Waziiya in Taiz

“One of the missiles landed near the runway minutes before the Yemeni flight from Cairo was to land,” it said. “We cancelled the landing of the incoming flight from Cairo [in Egypt] and diverted its route to Jeddah [in Saudi Arabia] to protect the passengers.”

The ministry also said it evacuated the airport terminal and removed two planes from the tarmac during the attacks.

It added, “This incident could easily have turned a civilian flight into a horrific humanitarian disaster, claiming the lives of dozens of innocent people in an instant.”

Aden airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control in the city that has been the seat of the government since the takeover of the capital, Sanaa, by the Iran-supported group in 2014.

The Houthis said in a statement they targeted “Saudi military supplies” arriving at the Badr camp near the airport with ballistic missiles. Saudi Arabia backs Yemen’s government.

Separately, the Saudi-led military coalition fighting in Yemen said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile, launched by the Houthis, north of Riyadh.

In a social media post, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, said it was tracking the launch platform used in the attack via an intelligence system over Sanaa, and promised to destroy it.

The Houthis said in statements on Tuesday and overnight into Wednesday that they had targeted Saudi international airports in Riyadh and Abha.

The intensified fighting in Yemen comes amid mounting regional tensions set off by the US-Israel war on Iran. The Saudi-backed government forces launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis to retake the Red Sea port of Mocha and areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Fighting has concentrated in the southwestern province of Taiz.

Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, described “all-out battles to take over the ground, the highlands and the mountains east of Bab al-Mandeb”.

“It’s a battle to take over the strategic western part of Taiz, and whoever controls the wider vicinity will overlook the region and have dominant military control,” he said.

“For the Yemeni government to take control of Mocha and the strategic bases and locations along the Red Sea coast, it first has to drive the Houthis off the mountains east of Mocha.”

Pakistan and Turkiye on Monday agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under their mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter Houthi attacks.

articles.title: Has Russia’s fuel crisis given Iranian oil an opening in Central Asia?
articles.summary: Iran's oil exports have struggled amid a US blockade. A Russian energy crisis because of Ukrainian attacks could help.
articles.preview: Iran’s oil exports have struggled amid a US blockade. A Russian energy crisis because of Ukrainian attacks could help. Countries in Central Asia have begun buying oil from Iran as the Russian fuel supplies they have long depended on run dry amid Ukraine’s mounting attacks on Russian energy infrastructure to degrade Moscow’s war effort. In August, Tajikistan announced it was receiving oil and petroleum products from Iran as Dushanbe faces uncertainty over its fuel supply from Russia.
articles.body:
Iran’s oil exports have struggled amid a US blockade. A Russian energy crisis because of Ukrainian attacks could help.

Countries in Central Asia have begun buying oil from Iran as the Russian fuel supplies they have long depended on run dry amid Ukraine’s mounting attacks on Russian energy infrastructure to degrade Moscow’s war effort.

In August, Tajikistan announced it was receiving oil and petroleum products from Iran as Dushanbe faces uncertainty over its fuel supply from Russia. Tehran also agreed to establish a joint refinery in Kyrgyzstan in August, and supply the country with crude oil.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

- list 1 of 3Trump pushes Russia-Ukraine ‘energy truce’: Can it work?

- list 2 of 3Russia’s Putin rules out ceasefire with Ukraine during speech in Moscow

- list 3 of 3G7 nations to release oil and diesel stocks, will it bring down the prices?

Moscow has been facing fuel shortages due to Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries as Russia’s war on its neighbour continues to rage.

Can the Russian fuel crisis give Iran a new oil opening in Central Asia?

Here’s what we know:

Which Central Asian countries have been affected by Russia’s fuel crisis?

Ukraine’s offensive against Russian energy infrastructure has caused panic across Central Asian countries like Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, which are dependent on Moscow for oil and petroleum products.

Tajikistan has traditionally sourced up to 80 percent of its petroleum products from Russia. Kyrgyzstan also relies on petroleum product imports, sourcing more than 90 percent of its petrol from Russia.

“They’ve been hurt the most,” Galiya Ibragimova, a Moldova-based expert on Central Asia with Carnegie Politika, which has its headquarters in Berlin, told Al Jazeera in an interview in August.

Kyrgyzstan is a member of the Eurasian Economic Union, the free trade bloc of five former Soviet nations dominated by Russia and the Kremlin’s political decisions.

Tajikistan is not a member of the group, but it bought discounted Russian fuel as “payment for political loyalty, not because [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is so kind”, Ibragimova added.

Kazakhstan, meanwhile, boasts three giant, Soviet-era oil refineries. Still, fuel prices in the country have increased by 15.6 percent this year, the UlusMedia website reported on July 10.

Uzbekistan, on the other hand, is less dependent on Russian energy, with domestic production capable of reaching 100,000 tonnes of petroleum products per month, satisfying most of the country’s needs. But due to the increase in oil demand from its regional neighbours, Uzbekistan has also been forced to diversify its imports and has begun striking deals with countries like Georgia and Iraq.

Why is there a fuel crisis in Russia?

Russia has been facing a severe fuel deficit as Kyiv’s drone strikes – launched in an effort to degrade Moscow’s ability to maintain its ongoing invasion of Ukraine – have knocked out an estimated quarter to half of its total oil refining capacity.

To tackle the problem, Russia has imposed fuel rationing. Sales are often limited to about 20-30 litres (about 5-8 US gallons) per vehicle, and drivers must pump fuel strictly into vehicle tanks. Filling jerry cans is largely prohibited.

Earlier, the government banned petrol and jet fuel exports. Officials are now weighing a ban on diesel exports, too. Authorities have loosened fuel-quality regulations, temporarily allowing lower-grade fuel for the domestic market.

A state of emergency has also been declared in Russian-occupied Crimea, which Moscow annexed from Ukraine in 2014. A Russian-owned oil firm in India, Nayara Energy, has reportedly sold petroleum to Russia.

While Russian President Putin acknowledges the crisis, he appears reluctant to end the war on Ukraine and insists the situation is under control.

“These attacks on our facilities certainly create problems – that is obvious. We are currently seeing a certain shortage, though I would say it is not critical,” he said earlier this year.

“First and foremost, we have to rapidly and significantly increase production of air defence systems that are most in demand. We must also continue to improve them… Repairs at refineries must be completed more quickly.”

So, how is Iran helping Central Asia?

Amid Russian fuel shortages, Central Asian countries like Tajikistan have begun striking deals with Iran.

In August, Tajikistan’s Energy and Water Resources Ministry told the Asia-Plus news agency that the country is receiving oil and petroleum products from Iran. The ministry has not disclosed the route used to transport the products, but Tajikistan expects to receive 2.55 million tonnes of oil and petroleum products from Iran.

Besides Tajikistan, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian welcomed a proposal from Kyrgyzstan in August to establish a joint refinery in the Central Asian country, according to a report by Iran’s Tasnim news agency,

Under the agreement, Pezeshkian said, “The crude oil needed by the refinery can be supplied by Iran, and the products can be divided between the two sides.”

Will exporting oil to Central Asian countries help Iran?

The United States and Israel’s war on Iran has affected Tehran’s oil revenues. Data released by the government-administered Statistical Center of Iran in September showed that gross domestic product (GDP) shrank by 10.1 percent year-on-year between March 21 and June 20, the first quarter of the Persian calendar.

Tehran’s ability to sell crude has also been dramatically curtailed by the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, imposed for most of the war, which began in late February.

Iranian crude and condensate loadings collapsed from about two million barrels per day (bpd) in March to roughly 740,000bpd in July and just 220,000-255,000bpd in August, according to estimates from Kpler and Vortexa.

TankerTrackers.com told the Reuters news agency in September that 29 tankers, carrying 36.11 million barrels of crude, were trapped in the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Vortexa estimated that total Iranian crude afloat had fallen from 135 million barrels at the end of July to 107 million barrels by late August.

Amid these challenges, Iran has been scrambling to find new countries to trade oil with. Russian fuel shortages have opened up new opportunities for Iran in Central Asia, at least in the short term, according to analysts.

How does Iranian oil reach Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan?

Iran does not share a border with either country.

To get to Tajikistan, Iranian “oil and refined products have to cross Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan by rail”, said Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs.

To get to Kyrgyzstan, Iranian oil would also need to pass through Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

Is trading oil with Iran logistically sustainable for Central Asia?

It is unlikely, Schneider said.

“This opportunity [for Iran] depends on Ukraine continuing to hit Russian refineries, which seems unlikely, both given the waning of Ukraine’s strike capability and the US government’s demand to stop the attacks as they put too much strain on global oil markets,” he told Al Jazeera.

He noted that US President Donald Trump has pressed his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, repeatedly in September for an “energy truce” with Russia, since diesel prices have become a political problem for Trump ahead of the November midterm elections in the US.

“Those truces have so far collapsed within hours, but the direction is clear. Once the strikes stop, or once Russia repairs its plants, Russian fuel will come back to Central Asia duty-free under Eurasian Economic Union arrangements, and Iran will struggle to compete on price,” he said.

Logistics also favour Russia with respect to importing oil to countries like Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, he said.

Unlike Iran, Russia shares a border with both.

“Tajikistan’s own request [for oil] would need around 51,000 rail tank cars, and its main refinery at Dangara has never operated commercially at scale. Russia, by contrast, has decades’ worth of logistics infrastructure, pipelines, rail links, and supply contracts into the region,” Schneider said.

Is Central Asia a big enough market to compensate for Iran’s Hormuz losses?

No, according to Schneider.

Tajikistan’s total demand, Schneider said, was about 50,000bpd.

That is a drop in the ocean compared with the 1.7 million bpd Iran exported by sea a year ago. China reported $9.96bn in two-way trade with Iran in 2025, a figure that does not include some $31.2bn in Iranian oil shipments, according to the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission.

“This suggests that Central Asia can be a useful outlet for Iranian diesel and gasoline, but it cannot replace the Chinese market,” Schneider said.

For Tehran, Central Asia’s importance depends on how the US-Israel war on Iran develops, he said, adding that Tehran also needs to stay on good terms with Russia, with which it has a deep strategic partnership.

“Iran cannot afford to be seen as poaching Russian customers too aggressively, so it will present itself as a stopgap supplier, which, again, limits how much it can earn there,” he said.

What other risks does Central Asia face in buying Iranian oil?

Schneider warned that Central Asian nations could be hit with Washington’s secondary sanctions on Iran.

“Legally, US secondary sanctions apply to any foreign company or bank that conducts a significant transaction in Iranian petroleum, wherever it is based, and the Treasury expanded the list of sanctionable conduct in August. A Treasury official has already warned publicly that anyone in this trade ‘incurs that risk themselves’,” he noted.

But Schneider said that, politically, the US sanctioning Central Asian governments is unlikely.

“Central Asia is the arena of a new ‘Great Game’ between Russia, China and the United States, and Washington is courting the region harder than at any point since the 1990s, chiefly for its critical minerals. Kazakhstan alone holds about half of the minerals the US classifies as critical, including uranium and tungsten,” he said.

“Sanctioning a Central Asian government for buying fuel from Iran would push them straight back into closer ties to Russia and China,” he noted.

“What I would expect instead are targeted designations of individual traders, rail and logistics operators and smaller banks, combined with quiet pressure on the region’s correspondent banks. That alone is enough to raise the cost and slow the trade, but will come at the price of these countries redoubling their efforts to decouple economically and financially from the US.”

articles.title: Israele ricorda il 7 ottobre, il fallimento al centro delle elezioni
articles.summary: Il Paese si è spostato a destra, pochi credono che il terrorismo sia sconfitto
articles.preview: Nel terzo anniversario del massacro del 7 ottobre, Israele si prepara ad una settimana di commemorazioni, eventi, proteste e cortei. La biciclettina senza pedali di Ariel Bibas, il bambino dai capelli rossi diventato un simbolo di quella giornata di orrore, sarà alla mostra 'The Space Left Behind', una raccolta di oggetti appartenuti a coloro che sono stati uccisi, presi in ostaggio, colpiti dagli eventi. Ariel fu rapito dalla Jihad con il fratellino Kfir di nove mesi e la mamma Shiri. Nessuno dei tre è tornato dalla prigionia a Gaza.
articles.body:
Nel terzo anniversario del massacro del 7 ottobre, Israele si prepara ad una settimana di commemorazioni, eventi, proteste e cortei. La biciclettina senza pedali di Ariel Bibas, il bambino dai capelli rossi diventato un simbolo di quella giornata di orrore, sarà alla mostra 'The Space Left Behind', una raccolta di oggetti appartenuti a coloro che sono stati uccisi, presi in ostaggio, colpiti dagli eventi.

Ariel fu rapito dalla Jihad con il fratellino Kfir di nove mesi e la mamma Shiri. Nessuno dei tre è tornato dalla prigionia a Gaza. Se non fosse stato ucciso, il 5 agosto avrebbe compiuto 7 anni.

Il fallimento dell'apparato di sicurezza e del governo guidato da Benjamin Netanyahu continua a torturare gli israeliani. Il 27 ottobre si vota. Il sentimento di lutto, frustrazione, la nostalgia di figli e genitori persi faranno la loro parte nelle urne. Le prime elezioni in Israele dopo la mattanza di Hamas - e la successiva offensiva militare che ha provocato decine di migliaia di morti palestinesi a Gaza - si portano dietro il peso della peggiore strage di civili ebrei dalla Shoah e le considerazioni politiche che ne conseguono.

Le responsabilità per non aver previsto, interpretato i segnali che arrivavano dalla Striscia gravano sulla candidatura dell'attuale primo ministro. Che si è ripresentato, nonostante l'età, il cancro e i 19 anni di premierato, seppur con interruzioni, che ne fanno il premier più longevo nella storia del Paese. Unico a non aver ammesso le sue responsabilità per la strage, diversamente dall'ex capo dell'Idf Herzi Halevi e l'ex direttore dello Shin Bet Ronen Bar.

Al centro della campagna elettorale finiscono regolarmente vecchie e nuove accuse lanciate dai media israeliani anti-Bibi e dalle testate internazionali per contestargli di essere stato avvisato della catastrofe che stava per abbattersi su Israele, ma di non averci prestato attenzione. Tuttavia lo zoccolo duro dei 'bibisti', i più tenaci sostenitori di Netanyahu, non sembra avere intenzione di fare marcia indietro neppure davanti al precipizio, anche di reputazione, in cui è piombata la nazione con la guerra a Gaza.

Dopo il 7 ottobre, Israele non è più lo stesso di prima. Tra gli effetti di quella giornata in cui furono uccisi 1.200 civili e altri 251 presi in ostaggio, gli analisti indicano un evidente spostamento a destra. Secondo un sondaggio dell'Israel defence and security forum, uno dei cambiamenti più marcati si è registrato sulla questione dello Stato palestinese: se nel settembre 2023 il 31% degli intervistati riteneva che sarebbe stato un disastro per Israele, oggi la percentuale è salita al 52%. Il 52% pensava che fosse necessario raggiungere un accordo 'con una leadership palestinese seria', oggi la percentuale è crollata al 31%.

Da una diversa ricerca dell'Institute for National Security emerge un forte scetticismo nella percezione della sicurezza, argomento ritenuto esistenziale. Gli israeliani non pensano che a Gaza sia stata ottenuta una vittoria: il 59% oggi stima che un evento simile al 7 ottobre potrebbe ripetersi nei prossimi anni al confine con la Striscia. Però c'è da dire che non tutti vanno a destra. La mappa dei rilevamenti elettorali svela una piccola rinascita della sinistra israeliana: nell'attuale Knesset, eletta nel 2022, è rappresentata solo da 4 deputati, mentre il partito dei Democratici di Yair Golan adesso viaggia intorno ai 10 seggi.

I numeri parlano abbastanza chiaro, ma il sentimento delle persone è un altro mondo. E sbuca improvvisamente, quando meno te lo aspetti. Capita di chiedere un caffè ristretto in un bar di Tel Aviv, subito scatta la battuta sugli italiani e la tazzina, poi le chiacchiere sul gusto, i sapori. E così, incidentalmente, prima di andare via quel signore con le rughe precoci tira fuori un ricordo. Anche al figlio piaceva il caffè italiano, è stato ucciso dai terroristi al festival Nova, ci era andato per lavorare da cameriere. Aveva 20 anni.

Mercoledì Israele si sveglierà presto. Alle 6.29 del mattino ci sarà un minuto di silenzio, l'ora in cui iniziò l'attacco. Alle 7 gli attivisti si raduneranno davanti alle case dei ministri che erano in carica quel giorno. Le due cerimonie dello Stato sono fissate per il 5 del mese. Il Consiglio del 7 ottobre ha parlato con una sola voce per tutti: 'A distanza di tre anni, questa data non deve diventare solo un altro giorno sul calendario. Dietro i numeri ci sono persone, famiglie, vite spezzate, e dietro la tragedia ci sono ancora domande. Il popolo israeliano merita risposte'.

articles.title: Residents of kibbutz destroyed in 7 October Hamas-led attacks grapple with how to rebuild
articles.summary: Three years on from the attack on Nir Oz, in which 47 people were killed and 76 taken hostage, some survivors have returned to live there.
articles.preview: Roosting birds now coo among the ceiling tiles in the deserted dining room of Kibbutz Nir Oz, once the bustling heart of a close-knit, 400-strong Israeli community which was devastated by the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023. "We used to come and see each other, eat together. There were lots of activities here, also holidays to celebrate," remembers Dalit Ram Aharon, who is showing me around with her husband, Achi. By the glass entrance doors, dotted with bullet holes, there is a shocking reminder of what happened to the missing residents.
articles.body:
Roosting birds now coo among the ceiling tiles in the deserted dining room of Kibbutz Nir Oz, once the bustling heart of a close-knit, 400-strong Israeli community which was devastated by the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023.

"We used to come and see each other, eat together. There were lots of activities here, also holidays to celebrate," remembers Dalit Ram Aharon, who is showing me around with her husband, Achi.

By the glass entrance doors, dotted with bullet holes, there is a shocking reminder of what happened to the missing residents.

The postboxes for each household bear stickers put there after the attacks three years ago: red indicates those killed, and black those taken hostage. "That's one out of four of us: murdered or kidnapped," Dalit says. "Including children and babies."

As Israel marks the third anniversary of its deadliest-ever day, this is another painful time of reflection for residents of the kibbutz, which sits just a mile (1.6km) from the Gaza border and was one of the worst-hit places.

Time stands still at the nearby burnt-out house of the Siman Tov family, where a wind chime dangles by the door. A picture shows Tamar and Yonatan with their three children, twin girls Shahar and Arbel, five, and their two-year-old son, Omer.

The parents were shot through the door of their bomb shelter - designed to protect from rockets launched from Gaza, not gunfire.

Dalit, who survived with Achi and their three children by hiding in their own shelter for nearly 12 hours that day, recalls the last social media messages sent by Tamar to her neighbours.

"On that day in the morning, she wrote in the woman's group, at the beginning, 'Is everyone fine?' Then, at another point, she wrote, 'They are shooting us.' And after that she wrote with a lot of mistakes, 'We are very injured,'" Dalit tells me.

"From what we understand, they torched the house and the children died from suffocation, so all the family was killed."

An estimated 500 Palestinians, led by Hamas's elite Nukhba force fighters, but including civilian looters, some of them children, joined the assault on the unsuspecting Nir Oz.

Forty-one Nir Oz residents and foreign workers were killed, along with six people who had fled to the kibbutz from a party nearby.

Seventy-six people from the kibbutz were kidnapped to Gaza, including nine bodies, with 14 hostages taken alive and killed in captivity. The last living hostages from Nir Oz were returned to Israel on 13 October 2025 and the remains of the last deceased hostage, Amiram Cooper, were brought back two weeks later.

As we walk through the greenery, it is eerily quiet bar bird song and the mewing of hungry, stray cats. Dozens of fire-damaged homes, which were simple, one-storey buildings in Nir Oz, have now been torn down, leaving just rows of the reinforced concrete safe rooms, which failed to keep people safe.

The Aharons want some damaged houses to be left as evidence of what took place. "We really support that," Achi says. "People should see what happened, should see the destruction, the pure hatred that happened here."

The couple point out where a teacher, Maya Goren, was killed while in the kindergarten and the makeshift memorials where three of the seven members of the kibbutz security team were killed after battling Hamas gunmen.

The findings of the Israeli Defense Forces investigation into what happened at Nir Oz underscored how the army - left in a state of disarray by the unprecedented simultaneous assault on more than 20 communities and multiple military posts - completely failed to come to the rescue here.

On 7 October, the first soldiers arrived in the kibbutz some 40 minutes after the last Palestinian attackers left. Nearly every household experienced killing, violence, including sexual assaults and rape, looting and kidnapping.

Dalit pauses to show me a tree planted long ago by her parents, who were co-founders of the kibbutz, known for its farming and peace activists. They survived the 7 October attacks physically unharmed but died just months afterwards.

Next door is the small home of Shiri Bibas, the mother of ginger-haired boys Ariel, four, and nine-month-old, Kfir. The three, snatched from their home, became symbols of the Gaza hostage crisis.

"This is the hardest house for me because Shiri was a very, very good friend of mine," Dalit confides. "She was like a sister. We even got pregnant together - me with my daughter and her with Ariel. They became best friends also. We used to laugh that they were going to marry."

"Shiri was very, very funny. She was a happy person - a mother," Dalit says. "She lived a simple life. She never did anything to anyone."

While Shiri's husband, Yarden, was released alive by Hamas in a Gaza ceasefire deal in February 2025, she and her sons - held by a different armed group - were killed.

Hamas blamed an air strike early in the Gaza war for their deaths, but Israeli forensic experts, who examined the bodies after they were returned later that February, said they were murdered by their captives and their bodies mutilated.

Many of the bereaved from Nir Oz, including Yarden Bibas, have moved away for good. However, with 20 houses renovated or rebuilt, a few former hostages have come back to live here.

They include Gadi Moses, another kibbutz co-founder, and the oldest living male hostage released during the Gaza war, and Yair Horn, who stops to chat with the Aharons as he passes in a golf buggy. Dalit and Achi are determined to return too.

"We'll come back for the memory of Shiri and for the people that didn't have the chance to live here, and for the memory of my parents, and to continue our roots, and for my children, because this is our home," Dalit says.

However, she, Achi and their children - currently displaced and living in an apartment in a town further north - face a two-year wait for Nir Oz to reopen fully.

"Terrorists penetrated 97% of the households and burned down almost 50%," says Emi Palmor, director of the rebuilding project. "Now it's the only place in Israel that has to be completely demolished and completely replanned."

She says that it is a difficult balance to redesign the kibbutz so that it feels like home but does not cause new trauma to those who return.

"It's a huge debate â a very painful debate," Emi says. "Some people say, 'If I come back here, I want the entire area to look serene. I don't have to be reminded because I remember every day the people I lost.' Other people say, 'There is such denial â if we will take down the last houses, who will ever believe?'"

About 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage after an estimated 6,000 Palestinians streamed across the Gaza border during the attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023.

The ensuing war between Israel and Hamas has killed more than 74,200 people in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose overall figures are seen as accurate by the UN.

Despite the US-brokered ceasefire deal which brought the last hostages home a year ago, violence has continued, including near-daily Israeli attacks on Gaza. Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced and much of the territory is in ruins. US President Donald Trump's peace plan is at an impasse.

For Israelis, there are outstanding questions over accountability for the failure of Israel's security forces to have prevented the 7 October attacks. People from Nir Oz favour a comprehensive state commission of inquiry and still have major security concerns.

Survivors, including the Aharons, suffer from post-traumatic stress. Dalit recalls how her eldest son, Uri, turned nine on 7 October 2023 - when they spent the day hiding in their bomb shelter. "He told me, 'Mum, I don't want to die on my birthday,'" she says. "You know people don't understand that we still live this horrible day."

This anniversary of the attacks is the first with no hostages remaining in Gaza. "It's a very big relief," Dalit says. Achi sees that now is the time to focus on personal healing.

"Until the hostages came back, it was the only thing on our mind," he says. "Now you have the time to concentrate on yourself, on what you lost, what you need. Now it's our recovery or some kind of recovery as much as we can."

“El 7 de octubre de 2023, estaba seguro de que pagaríamos un precio muy alto y de que nuestras vidas acabarían destrozadas. Realmente lo sentía. Y es lo que ha sucedido”. articles.body:
La battaglia nel Mar Nero, che ha già visto decine di imbarcazioni colpite da droni nell'ultimo anno, ha subito un'ulteriore impennata nelle ultime ore, con due navi cargo colpite al largo della Bulgaria, di cui una affondata, con l'equipaggio che risulta disperso. Lunedì, invece, un altro mercantile si era inabissato al largo della Romania, provocando la morte del capitano e di un altro membro dell'equipaggio, entrambi cittadini dell'Azerbaigian.

Le autorità bulgare e rumene non hanno precisato la provenienza dei droni. Ma Russia e Ucraina continuano i pesanti bombardamenti reciproci, in particolare sulle rispettive capitali. Nella notte tra lunedì e martedì la regione di Mosca è stata bersagliata con uno degli attacchi più massicci degli ultimi mesi, che ha visto impiegati 650 droni, secondo il sindaco Serghei Sobyanin.

Lo stesso primo cittadino ha aggiunto che la maggior parte dei velivoli sono stati abbattuti, ma il governatore della regione, Andrei Vorobyov, ha detto che due uomini, di 20 e di 71 anni, sono morti e altre nove persone sono state ferite. Inoltre, tre persone sono rimaste uccise e tre ferite in un attacco delle forze ucraine contro un minibus nella parte della regione ucraina di Zaporizhzhia sotto controllo russo, secondo quanto ha detto il capo dell'amministrazione filorussa, Evgeny Balitsky.

In Ucraina, invece, l'operatore nazionale della rete elettrica ha disposto blackout a rotazione a Kiev a seguito dei recenti attacchi russi alle infrastrutture energetiche. Mentre si è cominciato per la prima volta a installare reti antidrone sui ponti nella capitale, dopo i ripetuti attacchi di Mosca nei giorni scorsi contro gli attraversamenti sul fiume Dnipro in città. Nelle ultime ore, un altro attacco ad un ponte sullo stesso fiume è stato registrato a Zaporizhzhia, dove il traffico è stato bloccato e sono segnalati cinque feriti.

Le due navi mercantili attaccate nel Mar Nero nella zona economica esclusiva bulgara, appartengono ad armatori turchi, secondo il database del trasporto marittimo Equasis, citato dall'agenzia Afp. Non si sa quanti fossero i membri dell'equipaggio su quella affondata, la Alfa Watan, che risultano dispersi.

Dopo una riunione d'emergenza del suo governo, il primo ministro bulgaro, Rumen Radev, ha detto che è al momento impossibile indicare da quale parte provenissero i droni che hanno colpito le navi. Si è trattato, ha sottolineato il premier, di "un attacco assolutamente inaccettabile nella zona economica esclusiva bulgara, una gravissima violazione del diritto internazionale e delle norme marittime".

Anche la nave affondata lunedì nella zona economica esclusiva romena, la Royad Mammadov, era di proprietà turca. Nella serata di martedì un incendio è scoppiato al largo della città russa di Sochi. Le fiamme e un'alta colonna di fumo erano visibili a distanza di chilometri. Fonti ucraine hanno parlato di un attacco con droni a una petroliera. Mentre testimoni sul posto sentiti dall'ANSA ritengono che sia stata colpita una infrastruttura per il trasbordo di petrolio.

articles.title: Fear and disruption for Ukraine's rail passengers as Russia escalates drone attacks
articles.summary: Ukrainians travelling by train are increasingly caught in the crosshairs of Russia's attacks.

But attacks are intensifying, with more than half of all strikes on locomotives since then occurring this year alone, according to the state-owned operator. articles.body:
Ukraine's railways have kept the country running since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. But attacks are intensifying, with more than half of all strikes on locomotives since then occurring this year alone, according to the state-owned operator.

Yuliia Ponomarenko, 27, a marketing specialist from Kharkiv, found her journey to Warsaw last month suddenly interrupted just short of the Ukraine-Poland frontier.

"The border guards started running around and shouting "Run! Get out of the carriages! There's shelling!"

A Russian drone had just hit a locomotive near the same border, and a special train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European dignitaries, had passed through minutes before.

Passengers on Yuliia's train were kept waiting for six hours while the fire up ahead was put out and the line cleared, she says: "We were really lucky that we were delayed a little and it wasn't our train."

She is among an increasing number of Ukrainian passengers facing disruption and long delays, as air raid alerts trigger emergency evacuations far from the battlegrounds of the east.

In September alone, 5,831 trains had to be evacuated due to Russian drone attacks, state owned railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia told AFP news agency on Monday. This meant on average each day, 205 trains were stopped.

It appears to be part of a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure, with two bridges attacked in Kyiv in the past few days and passengers of a metro train caught up in one of the strikes.

Seventeen-year-old Anastasiia Ryvbalchenko has also experienced a narrow escape.

She and her fellow passengers were forced to leave their train at 4am, towards the end of a long of a journey from Odesa to Kirovohrad on 16 September.

"On my way to Odesa, there had been a lot of evacuations and now on my way back it was happening again," she says. "I was already thinking that if there was another evacuation, I just couldn't take it any more."

An hour and a half later, as passengers waited in the dark, a drone struck nearby.

"There was an extremely loud explosion and everyone started running into the woods," she said.

It is not clear what the target was, and in this case the train was not damaged, but with further explosions lighting up the night sky, Anastasiia decided not to linger, continuing her journey on foot before being picked up by her parents.

"I'm not going to travel by train anymore," she says.

Anastassia's journey was more dramatic than most, but delays â some brief, others that last for hours â are now commonplace.

Since Russian drones first started attacking moving passenger trains towards the end of 2025, the routine for passengers has become increasingly familiar: leave the train, scroll Telegram channels for updates on drone and missile launches, send messages to warn friends and family that the train is delayed.

For a railway company proud of its record for punctuality, this year's disrupted schedule is posing a major challenge.

"We used to say that that during times of war we performed better than some railways in Europe in regular times,"the head of rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia, Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, told us.

"But now the life of our passengers and crew members is the utmost priority."

Russia's defence ministry denies targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.

The dangers are very real. Attacks on Ukrzaliznytsia's rolling stock and stations have risen sharply.

Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, almost 60% have been this year, according to statistics released by the company. Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.

"The latest wave of escalation and real war with railways is becoming extremely intense," said Pertsovskyi.

"It's a combination of the deadly force of their shahed drones and precision that they achieve with cameras and mesh networks so they can hit moving targets."

According to Pertsovskyi, some of Russia's most recent drones are equipped with AI tools and image recognition. Ukraine is understandably cagey about how it goes about confronting this increasingly sophisticated threat, but electronic methods to disrupt the drones' connectivity are high on the list.

"Unfortunately, this is always a cat-and-mouse game," he said.

- Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign

- Published7 days ago

We were given rare access to an underground bunker in Kyiv, dubbed â appropriately enough â the "Iron Command Centre", where railway staff monitor threats in real time.

On one huge video screen, colour-coded passenger and freight trains could be seen making their way along the arteries of Ukraine's vast railway network.

We watched as a red icon representing a drone appeared to loiter over Kyiv, practically above our heads at one point.

Each drone had a 100km (62-mile) circle around it. Any passenger trains inside the circle would already have been evacuated, with customers not allowed to reboard until the train was outside the circle and the drone was still moving away.

"Our mission is not to let our train or our crew members be in that immediate attack area," Pertsovskyi said.

The company's precautions appear to have kept casualties low. Its figures for 2026 show that eight company employees have been killed, six of them when a ballistic missile struck a locomotive depot in Kyiv.

During our visit to Iron Command, another air raid siren sounded in Kyiv. The city's main railway station, we were told, was being evacuated.

On a later visit to the busy station, we found passengers waiting outside the main entrance or sheltering in underground passageways. Over the tannoy came news of steady stream of delays.

Everyone knows the coming months could be among the most difficult yet.

With winter not far off, Ukrzaliznytsia is already figuring out how to deal with evacuations when the outside temperature can reach -20C or below and snow is lying heavy on the ground.

Along with international donors, the company is preparing winter evacuation packs, mobile shelters and bus services in areas where evacuations become too frequent.

"We might be a slightly different railway, a reinvented railway," Pertsovskyi said. "But we'll keep connecting the country, no matter what, be it winter, be it summer, no matter how hard the enemy hits us."

articles.summary: Ospite di Porta a Porta, il leader di Futuro Nazionale ha fatto intendere che gran parte delle colpe non sarebbero della Russia, ma è una ricostruzione parziale
articles.preview: Il 29 settembre il presidente di Futuro Nazionale Roberto Vannacci è stato ospite di Porta a Porta, su Rai1, dove ha commentato i risultati delle elezioni suppletive a Reggio Calabria e le principali questioni del dibattito politico. articles.body:
Il 29 settembre il presidente di Futuro Nazionale Roberto Vannacci è stato ospite di Porta a Porta, su Rai1, dove ha commentato i risultati delle elezioni suppletive a Reggio Calabria e le principali questioni del dibattito politico. Tra le altre cose, Vannacci è tornato ad affrontare il tema della guerra in Ucraina, ribadendo la necessità di interrompere il sostegno militare al governo di Volodymir Zelensky.

A sostegno della sua posizione, Vannacci ha ricostruito (-1:29:40) quelle che sarebbero le cause del nuovo conflitto in Ucraina, iniziato dopo l’invasione russa partita il 24 febbraio 2022. «I problemi tra l’Ucraina e la Russia sono cominciati nel 2008 in seguito al vertice della NATO che ha invitato l’Ucraina ad aderire alla NATO», ha detto Vannacci. Secondo il leader di Futuro Nazionale, in quel vertice ci sarebbe stato «l’avvio delle trattative» per l’adesione non solo dell’Ucraina, ma della Georgia e della Moldavia, cosa che non sarebbe stata gradita dal presidente russo Vladimir Putin, che temeva l’allargamento a Est dell’Organizzazione del Trattato dell’Atlantico del Nord (ossia la NATO, ndr). Vannacci ha poi aggiunto che la NATO e l’Ucraina non avrebbero accettato tre «ultimatum» dati da Putin prima dell’invasione. «L’Ucraina non entra nella NATO, non vengono schierate truppe della NATO in Ucraina, non vengono schierati sistemi a lunga gittata della NATO in Ucraina», queste sono le condizioni che Putin avrebbe dato secondo Vannacci e che però non sarebbero state accettate.

Ma le cose stanno davvero così? In breve: Vannacci semplifica troppo le cause del conflitto in Ucraina, creando una narrazione non supportata nel complesso dalle fonti ufficiali. L’affermazione secondo cui i problemi tra Russia e Ucraina sarebbero cominciati nel 2008, in seguito alla decisione della NATO di aprire all’ingresso dell’Ucraina, contiene una parte di verità ma la tesi secondo cui la NATO e l’Ucraina non avrebbero accettato gli “ultimatum” di Putin è fuorviante.

articles.title: Un pappagallo dopato che si specchia
articles.summary: Quando vogliamo definire e descrivere l’ultimo prodotto delle tecnologie digitali non riusciamo a fare meno di metafore più o meno indovinate, a partire da quella che si è diffusa di più: “intelligenza artificiale”
articles.preview: Il 31 agosto 1955 quattro ricercatori statunitensi, John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester e Claude Shannon, firmarono la proposta per un seminario estivo da tenere l’anno dopo al Dartmouth college, nel New Hampshire. Nel titolo del seminario c’era un’espressione nuova: “intelligenza artificiale”. Settantuno anni dopo possiamo dire che l’espressione è particolarmente indovinata e, allo stesso tempo, che ci ha creato un sacco di problemi.
articles.body:
Il 31 agosto 1955 quattro ricercatori statunitensi, John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester e Claude Shannon, firmarono la proposta per un seminario estivo da tenere l’anno dopo al Dartmouth college, nel New Hampshire. Nel titolo del seminario c’era un’espressione nuova: “intelligenza artificiale”.

Settantuno anni dopo possiamo dire che l’espressione è particolarmente indovinata e, allo stesso tempo, che ci ha creato un sacco di problemi. È stata anche la prima metafora di una lunga serie di modi di dire che usiamo per riferirci a queste tecnologie.

Se vogliamo essere rigorosi, alcune di queste espressioni sono metafore in senso stretto, come quando si parla di “allucinazioni” dei modelli linguistici. Altre, invece, sono analogie. Ma il linguista George Lakoff e il filosofo Mark Johnson, in Metafora e vita quotidiana, ci hanno tolto dall’imbarazzo e le hanno riunite sotto l’etichetta “metafore concettuali”. Cioè, parole che usiamo per avvicinarci alla comprensione di una cosa attraverso un’altra cosa che conosciamo meglio.

Il problema delle metafore concettuali è che tendono a concentrarsi su una parte del funzionamento delle ia lasciando da parte tutto il resto. Qui ho provato a elencare in maniera critica le più diffuse.

Il pappagallo stocastico

È una delle espressioni più famose: nasce da un articolo del 2021 firmato da Emily Bender, Timnit Gebru, Angelina McMillan-Major e Margaret Mitchell. Funziona molto bene perché ricorda il meccanismo alla base dei large language model (llm): questi sistemi producono sequenze di parole plausibili in base alla probabilità, senza garanzie di corrispondenza con il mondo.

Qualcuno potrebbe obiettare che anche quel che dice una persona non dà nessuna garanzia di corrispondenza con il mondo, ma per ora lasciamo da parte queste considerazioni.

L’articolo, pubblicato online con l’emoji del pappagallo 🦜 nel titolo, parlava anche dei costi ambientali di modelli sempre più grandi e dei pregiudizi contenuti nei dati. Questa parte, purtroppo, si è persa quasi del tutto per strada, fagocitata dalla metafora stessa. Anni dopo, Emily Bender ha dovuto fare alcune precisazioni sul suo lavoro lamentando proprio questa dinamica, che ha fatto parecchi danni.

Nel frattempo, però, il pappagallo è diventato una metafora sempre più stretta: i comportamenti emergenti e le rappresentazioni interne ai modelli individuate da chi fa ricerca la rendono sempre meno vera. “È solo un pappagallo stocastico” (o “è solo statistica”) è diventata una frase per chiudere le discussioni proprio quando bisognerebbe aprirle, visto che con questi strumenti si possono fare tantissime cose.

I pappagalli veri, tra l’altro, ne escono particolarmente maltrattati visto che sono animali sociali e piuttosto intelligenti.

Allucinazioni e stronzate

“Allucinazione” dà un nome a un’esperienza che chiunque abbia usato un chatbot riconosce: la risposta falsa detta con sicurezza. Ma, se pensiamo al suo significato originario, ci suggerisce anche una mente che percepisce le cose in maniera alterata e ci fa pensare che l’errore dipenda da un guasto del sistema.

Eppure le risposte giuste degli llm e quelle sbagliate sono il frutto dello stesso identico meccanismo.

Nel 2024 i filosofi Michael Townsen Hicks, James Humphries e Joe Slater hanno proposto un’alternativa: i chatbot producono stronzate nel senso descritto da Harry Frankfurt in Stronzate. Un saggio filosofico. Significa che i discorsi delle macchine sono indifferenti alla verità. È un’immagine più precisa del loro funzionamento.

Anche questa, però, ha almeno due problemi: prima di tutto, attribuisce un atteggiamento – l’indifferenza – a qualcosa che non ne ha; poi ci fa credere che queste macchine siano inutili.

Il jpeg sfocato del web

Nel febbraio 2023 lo scrittore Ted Chiang ha paragonato ChatGpt, che era diventato pubblico da poco, a un jpeg sfocato del web. Cioè, un’immagine compressa, con una perdita di dettagli, che però conserva un’impressione di visione d’insieme. È una metafora efficace per spiegare perché le risposte delle ia sembrano giuste anche quando sono approssimative.

Il rischio è che ci faccia pensare che le ia siano degli hard disk, dei contenitori di copie più o meno sbiadite delle opere originali. La conservazione integrale dei dati di addestramento, invece, è un’eccezione rispetto al funzionamento generale.

Non solo: come al solito in questa prospettiva la sfocatura è considerata un difetto che mina alla base l’utilità degli strumenti. Invece esiste proprio perché le macchine non contengono i dati con cui sono state addestrate, ma solo una loro rappresentazione.

Il doping

Secondo alcuni, l’uso delle intelligenze artificiali per alcune attività, come la scrittura, è paragonabile al doping. Questa metafora è stata rilanciata a proposito del romanzo di Thélyson Orélien. La parte buona di questo parallelismo è che ci obbliga a chiederci quali regole vogliamo: dove finisce l’aiuto lecito? Dove comincia quello che non tolleriamo?

Allo stesso tempo dobbiamo ammettere che quel confine sarà sempre una convenzione, proprio come le sostanze vietate nello sport. Il doping, però, presuppone un giudizio morale (chi si dopa sta barando). E presuppone anche che esista una prestazione pulita e naturale da proteggere. Ma la scrittura ha sempre avuto molte mani: editor, correttrici, traduttrici, revisori, come ci ha ricordato anche Claudia Durastanti.

L’analogia si porta dietro anche le sue istituzioni: il test, la squalifica, la lista delle sostanze proibite, la denuncia pubblica, le accuse anonime, il dubbio, lo stigma a priori. E la metafora del doping si concentra su chi ha barato ma lascia sempre fuori chi scrive le regole e chi può doparsi senza essere scoperto perché tanto ha già una posizione di privilegio.

Lo specchio

La filosofa Shannon Vallor ha dedicato un libro del 2024, The Ai mirror, all’idea che questi sistemi ci restituiscano l’immagine dei nostri dati e dei nostri pregiudizi. È una metafora che abbiamo usato anche nella prefazione di Intelligenza artificiale, un libro curato da Internazionale.

Funziona perché, essendo addestrate con tutto quel che c’è di umano, le ia ci rispecchiano in tutto. Il limite, però, è la presunzione di innocenza dello specchio, oggetto passivo e neutro. Le ia sono costruite da poche aziende che scelgono dati, filtri, regole, comportamenti da premiare o da rigettare, domande a cui i modelli devono rifiutarsi di rispondere, limiti d’uso e prezzi.

Se le ia sono specchi, allora sono specchi deformanti, ma questo non viene detto a chi li usa. La metafora rischia di assolvere chi li produce, minimizzando il suo ruolo.

Lo stagista-copilota

Ethan Mollick, docente alla Wharton school dell’università della Pennsylvania, negli Stati Uniti, suggerisce da tempo di trattare i chatbot come una persona, un collega o uno stagista da seguire. Come indicazione di metodo funziona bene perché, in effetti, si delega solo quel che si è deciso prima, si controlla ogni risposta e si pubblica solo quello che è stato revisionato e di cui ci si assume per intero la responsabilità.

Però anche questo antropomorfizza il comportamento della macchina e presuppone un rapporto di lavoro in cui non c’è un lavoratore. Lo stagista è un abbonamento pagato a un oligopolio che fa scomparire le persone che lavorano davvero, spesso sottopagate. Anche i nomi scelti dai produttori a volte sono metafore: Copilot della Microsoft, per esempio, ricalca perfettamente questa relazione.

Le intelligenze aliene

Nello Cristianini, che insegna intelligenza artificiale all’università di Bath, nel Regno Unito, ha proposto di considerare queste macchine come “intelligenze aliene”. È una metafora efficace soprattutto perché ci permette di pensarle come strumenti diversi da noi, altri. Ma l’alieno ha il problema che poi finisce per essere visto come un’entità cattiva che vorrà dominarci.

Elettricità, petrolio o tecnologie culturali

Fin dal 2017 l’informatico Andrew Ng ha paragonato queste tecnologie all’elettricità. L’immagine dice qualcosa di vero sulla loro diffusione come infrastruttura, e insieme le fa sembrare ancora una volta inevitabili e neutre come un servizio pubblico per il bene comune.

“I dati sono il nuovo petrolio”, formula usata dal matematico Clive Humby nel 2006, è diventata, forse per puro caso o forse per un’intuizione straordinaria, l’analogia più precisa: estrazione, energia, acqua, territorio, potere sono tutte questioni che si intersecano nel mondo delle ia. A marzo del 2025 Henry Farrell, Alison Gopnik, Cosma Shalizi e James Evans hanno proposto di considerare i grandi modelli linguistici come tecnologie culturali e sociali, parenti strette della scrittura e della stampa, ma anche delle biblioteche, dei mercati e delle burocrazie.

Più o meno nello stesso periodo Arvind Narayanan e Sayash Kapoor hanno parlato di “tecnologia normale”. Queste sono le cornici argomentative più utili perché spostano lo sguardo da tutte le distrazioni da cui siamo bombardati alle istituzioni che organizzano la conoscenza e quindi ai ragionamenti sul potere. Anche in questo caso ci sono dei limiti: “normale” può diventare un modo per dirci che tutto sommato anche la concentrazione in poche mani è una cosa naturale. Le biblioteche che conosciamo, però, sono in gran parte pubbliche. Questa, forse, è la metafora più interessante di cui abbiamo bisogno.

Superintelligenze

L’ultima virata sulle parole da usare è quella di Trump, che ha deciso di chiamare questi strumenti “superintelligenze”, firmando addirittura un ordine esecutivo per abolire “intelligenze artificiali” da tutti i documenti ufficiali della sua amministrazione. È un favore alla Silicon valley che corre verso l’idea di una “singolarità”, cioè la creazione di una macchina che acquisisce coscienza e impara a migliorarsi da sola. È un favore anche alla paura e alla distopia e non fa altro che creare più confusione.

Ogni metafora, presa da sola, è un’approssimazione, una sfocatura, un errore, magari anche un’allucinazione. Usarle bene, tutte insieme, somiglia al modo in cui conviene usare i modelli di ia: con consapevolezza, cercando di avere una visione d’insieme, accettando che la nostra comprensione è spesso sfocata (probabilmente molto più spesso di quanto vorremmo) e che va bene così.

Le immagini che hanno avuto più successo, però, vengono tutte dagli uffici marketing di chi vende i prodotti, aiutati dal catastrofismo fantascientifico e dalla politica: l’agente di ia che ci distruggerà è quella che, ultimamente, funziona di più. Forse perché, tutto sommato, pensiamo che avesse ragione l’agente Smith?
